# Nibbānadhātu Sutta (Iti 44 (It 2.17 PTS It 38))

**ID:** Iti 44 (It 2.17 PTS It 38)  
**Section:** Itivuttaka (iti)  
**Collection:** Sutta  
**Title (Pali):** Nibbānadhātu Sutta  
**tipitaka.org (CST):** [https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0504m.mul1.xml](https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0504m.mul1.xml)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Nibbānadhātu Sutta* (Iti 44; PTS It 38–39) is a discourse in the *Itivuttaka* expounding the two facets or elements of quenching (*nibbānadhātu*): the *Nibbāna* element with residue remaining (*sa-upādisesā nibbānadhātu*) and the *Nibbāna* element without residue (*anupādisesā nibbānadhātu*) [Bodhi 2003; Anālayo 2010]. In the prose exposition, the element with residue describes a living arahant who has eradicated lust, hatred, and delusion, yet whose five sense faculties (*pañcindriyāni*) remain intact, experiencing agreeable and disagreeable sensations; the element without residue describes the state where all feelings and experiences cool down right here (*idheva sabbavedayitāni anabhinanditāni sītībhavissanti*) [Hwang 2005; Radich 2007; Pande 1974].

Scholars identify Iti 44 as the canonical *locus classicus* for this twofold formula, though it represents a unique and anomalous instance within the Pāli canon as the only text that directly formulates and discusses this overt contrast [Radich 2007]. Pande notes a doctrinal nuance between the prose and the verse portions of the sutta: while the prose seems to present the element without residue as attainable during life, the accompanying verse explicitly characterizes *anupādisesā* as pertaining to the beyond (*samparāyikā*), where all becomings cease entirely [Pande 1974]. This distinction has generated ongoing hermeneutical discussion: whereas classical Theravāda commentarial tradition equates the two respectively with the extinction of defilements in life (*kilesaparinibbāna*) and the remainderless cessation of the aggregates at death (*khandhaparinibbāna*), modern reformers such as Buddhadāsa have argued on the basis of Iti 44 that both terms refer to the living experience of arahants who "die to selfhood" before physical death [Kang 2012; Bodhi 2003].

**Sources**

- [Bodhi 2003] Bhikkhu Bodhi, Connected Discourses of the Buddha (2003) — Explanation of the two nibbānadhātu elements at It 38–39 and their commentarial treatment.
- [Anālayo 2010] Bhikkhu Anālayo, From Grasping to Emptiness (2010) — Note on sa-upādisesā and anupādisesā nibbānadhātu in Itivuttaka (It 38) and the living versus deceased arahant.
- [Hwang 2005] Soonil Hwang, Metaphor and Literalism in Buddhism: Doctrinal History of Nirvana (2005) — Analysis of saupādisesa nibbānadhātu describing the five faculties (pañcindriyāni) rather than aggregates.
- [Kang 2012] In-gun Kang, Buddhist-Christian Dialogue and Action in Theravada Countries (2012) — Buddhadāsa's interpretation of Nibbānadhātu Sutta against Buddhaghosa's post-mortem view.
- [Pande 1974] Govind Chandra Pande, Studies in the Origins of Buddhism (1974) — Analysis of the contrast between the prose and verse accounts of anupādisesā nibbānadhātu in sutta 44.
- [Radich 2007] Michael David Radich, The Somatics of Liberation: Ideas about Embodiment in Buddhism from its Origin to the Fifth Century C.E. (2007) — Discussion of Iti 44 as an anomalous canonical locus classicus for the two nibbānadhātu types.
